events.title: Hamas-led attack on southern Israel
events.summary: At dawn on 7 October 2023, during the Simchat Torah holiday, Hamas-led militants fired thousands of rockets and breached the Gaza perimeter fence at dozens of points, attacking army bases, kibbutzim, Sderot and the Nova music festival near Re'im. Israel initially put the dead at about 1,400; on 10 November 2023 its Foreign Ministry revised the toll to about 1,200 after unidentified remains were determined to be attackers (Times of Israel, Al Jazeera, NPR). Israeli officials counted more than 240 hostages in late 2023, standardised as 251 in 2024 (Washington Post). The IDF said it killed roughly 1,000 attackers inside Israel in the following days. The Gaza Health Ministry reported 232 Palestinians killed in Gaza by Israeli strikes on 7 October (Texas Public Radio). It was the deadliest single day for Israel since its founding; the cabinet declared a state of war the next morning.

perspectives.framing: Describes 7 October as a massacre and the worst attack on Jews since the Holocaust, a 'terrorist' assault on civilians that justified a war to destroy Hamas and recover the hostages; Israel names its campaign Operation Swords of Iron.

Calls the assault 'Operation Al-Aqsa Flood', presenting it as a legitimate act of resistance against occupation and blockade and a response to Israeli actions at Al-Aqsa Mosque and against prisoners; it disputes that fighters deliberately targeted civilians.

Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned the attacks and hostage-taking as unjustifiable while saying they 'did not happen in a vacuum', pointing to decades of occupation; the UN Commission of Inquiry later found war crimes committed by Palestinian armed groups on 7 October.
President Biden called the attack 'pure, unadulterated evil' and 'sheer evil', affirmed Israel's right to defend itself and sent naval forces to the region as a deterrent.

events.title: Israel declares war and launches air campaign on Gaza
events.summary: On 8 October 2023 Israel's security cabinet formally declared a state of war under Article 40 of Basic Law: The Government, effective from 6 am on 7 October and the first such declaration since 1973 (Lieber Institute, Library of Congress). The IDF mobilised about 360,000 reservists, Al Jazeera reported. Air strikes on Gaza expanded into a sustained campaign against what the IDF described as Hamas command centres, tunnels, rocket sites and operatives' homes across Gaza City and the north. On 9 October Defence Minister Yoav Gallant ordered a 'complete siege', saying there would be 'no electricity, no food, no fuel' (Times of Israel, Al Jazeera, Globes). Al Jazeera reported the Gaza Health Ministry counting more than 300 Palestinians killed by 8 October; the ministry's own evening report gave 370 killed and 1,788 injured, figures that rose by hundreds daily.

perspectives.framing: Frames the campaign as a defensive war of necessity against a 'terror army' embedded in civilian areas, with the stated aims of dismantling Hamas's military and governing capacity and returning the hostages; the siege was justified as lawful pressure on a 'terrorist' entity.

Portrays the strikes as indiscriminate 'aggression' and collective punishment of a besieged population, and the siege as a war crime; it vowed to keep fighting and to trade hostages for Palestinian prisoners.

OCHA and the Secretary-General warned that a total siege violated international humanitarian law, called for humanitarian access and urged all parties to protect civilians, while UN human-rights bodies criticised the scale of strikes on residential areas.
Warned against any displacement of Gazans into Sinai, called for restraint and for the opening of the Rafah crossing to aid, positioning itself as mediator.

events.location: Shebaa Farms / Mount Dov, Israel-Lebanon frontier
events.title: Hezbollah opens a northern front against Israel
events.summary: On 8 October 2023 Hezbollah fired guided rockets and artillery at three Israeli positions in the Shebaa Farms, which Lebanon claims and Israel has occupied since 1967, declaring that it acted 'in solidarity' with the Palestinian people; Israel answered with artillery barrages into southern Lebanon and no casualties were immediately reported (Al Jazeera, PBS, The Arab Weekly). The exchanges settled into a daily pattern of cross-border fire that Hezbollah described as a 'support front' calibrated to avoid full-scale war, while the IDF struck launch teams and commanders. From mid-October Israel evacuated communities along the border, a government-organised move covering more than 60,000 residents (Malay Mail/AFP, Deccan Herald/Reuters), and by February 2024 the fighting had displaced more than 90,000 people from southern Lebanon according to the Council on Foreign Relations' conflict tracker, citing UN migration-agency data. The front remained limited until the escalation of September 2024.

perspectives.framing: Presents its fire as a deliberately limited 'support front' for Gaza and an act of resistance against occupation, tied to a ceasefire in Gaza; it refers to Israel as 'the enemy entity'.

Regards the attacks as unprovoked aggression by an Iranian proxy that displaced tens of thousands of northern residents, and repeatedly warned it would push Hezbollah back beyond the Litani River in line with UN Security Council resolution 1701.
Insisted it did not seek war, appealed for de-escalation and international mediation, and blamed Israeli strikes for civilian deaths and displacement in the south.
UNIFIL and the UN Special Coordinator urged both sides to halt fire and respect resolution 1701, reporting damage to villages and peacekeeping positions.

events.title: Mass internal displacement across the Gaza Strip
events.summary: Late on 12 October 2023 the IDF informed the UN that the roughly 1.1 million residents of Gaza north of Wadi Gaza should move south within 24 hours ahead of its ground offensive (Reuters via US News, CNN, Al Jazeera). The UN said the order could not be carried out without devastating humanitarian consequences. Hundreds of thousands crowded into UNRWA schools, hospitals and tent camps further south and were displaced again by the Khan Younis offensive in December and the Rafah offensive in May 2024. In 2024 the UN and its partners estimated that at least 1.9 million people, nine in ten Gazans, had been internally displaced, many several times (UN OCHA, UNRWA, Human Rights Watch); by November 2024 OCHA put about 79 per cent of the Strip under active evacuation orders. Israel meanwhile evacuated tens of thousands from communities near Gaza and Lebanon.

perspectives.framing: Describes evacuation orders as measures to move civilians out of combat zones and away from Hamas positions, and designates 'humanitarian zones' such as al-Mawasi; it accuses Hamas of preventing civilians from leaving and of using them as human shields.
Together with Hamas, describes the displacement as a 'second Nakba' (the 1948 Palestinian displacement) and forced transfer aimed at emptying Gaza, and rejects any resettlement outside the territory.

OCHA and UNRWA call it the largest displacement of Palestinians since 1948, say no place in Gaza is safe, and report that shelters are overcrowded and repeatedly hit; UN officials warned that mass evacuation orders are incompatible with international humanitarian law when no safe destination exists.
Rejected any transfer of Gazans into Sinai as a liquidation of the Palestinian cause and a security threat, and kept the Rafah crossing open only for limited aid and evacuations.

events.title: Explosion at Al-Ahli Arab Hospital
events.summary: On the evening of 17 October 2023 an explosion in the courtyard of the Anglican-run Al-Ahli Arab Hospital in Gaza City, where displaced families sheltered, killed and injured large numbers of people. The Gaza Health Ministry said 471 people were killed, and Hamas attributed the blast to an Israeli air strike. The IDF said a rocket fired by Palestinian Islamic Jihad had misfired and fallen on the hospital, which Islamic Jihad denied. US intelligence assessed that Israel was not responsible and estimated 100 to 300 deaths; Canada's defence ministry reached the same conclusion. Human Rights Watch found on 26 November 2023 that the damage was consistent with a rocket-propelled munition of the kind used by Palestinian armed groups and 'highly unlikely' to have come from a large air-dropped bomb, while saying the toll could not be verified (HRW, Haaretz, L'Orient Today); Palestinian civil-society groups disputed its findings.

perspectives.framing: Called it a 'massacre' by an Israeli air strike and a war crime, and maintained the ministry's figure of 471 dead.
Presented intercepted communications and radar tracks to argue that a failed Islamic Jihad rocket launched from a nearby cemetery caused the blast, and accused Hamas of spreading a 'blood libel'.
The White House and intelligence community said available evidence indicated Israel was not responsible and that the toll was likely at the low end of estimates, while calling for restraint.

Human Rights Watch found the blast pattern inconsistent with a large Israeli aerial bomb and consistent with a rocket, called for an independent investigation and stressed that its findings did not exonerate any party of earlier or later hospital strikes.

events.title: Israel launches ground invasion of northern Gaza
events.summary: On the night of 27 October 2023 the IDF announced it was 'expanding' ground operations and moved armoured and infantry units into the northern Gaza Strip under an intensified bombardment that severed Gaza's telephone and internet links for more than a day (NPR, CBC, CNN). Israeli forces advanced along the coast and through Beit Hanoun and Jabalia and by early November had encircled Gaza City and reached the sea, splitting the territory along what became the Netzarim corridor. Prime Minister Netanyahu said on 28 October that the war had entered its 'second stage' (Globe and Mail, Gulf News). The Gaza Health Ministry reported 7,028 Palestinians killed as of 26 October (AFP via Malay Mail) and 7,326 on 27 October; UN OCHA estimated about 1.4 million displaced. The UN General Assembly that day called for a humanitarian truce.

perspectives.framing: Calls the ground offensive a necessary campaign to dismantle Hamas's 'terror infrastructure', including tunnels under hospitals and schools, and stresses that it warns civilians to evacuate; it rejects calls for a ceasefire as a victory for Hamas.
Describes the invasion as a genocidal 'aggression' against a besieged people and says its fighters are conducting 'resistance' operations against occupying forces.
The General Assembly's 27 October resolution called for an immediate humanitarian truce and unhindered aid; UN agencies warned of civil order breaking down and hospitals running out of fuel.
Backed Israel's right to pursue Hamas while pressing for humanitarian pauses, more aid through Rafah and adherence to the laws of war; it opposed a general ceasefire at this stage.

events.title: Israeli strikes on Jabalia refugee camp
events.summary: On 31 October 2023 Israeli aircraft struck a residential block in Jabalia, the largest refugee camp in the Gaza Strip, leaving large craters and collapsed apartment buildings; a further strike hit the camp the next day. The IDF said it had targeted and killed Ibrahim Biari, commander of Hamas's Central Jabalia Battalion whom it linked to the 7 October attack, together with dozens of fighters in an underground complex, and blamed the collapse of buildings on tunnels beneath them (CNBC, CNN). Hamas denied that a commander was present. The director of the nearby Indonesian Hospital said at least 80 people were killed and hundreds injured (CNN); the monitoring group Airwars later assessed at least 126 civilians killed, including 68 children, and cited munitions experts who identified 2,000-pound bombs. The UN human rights office said the strikes could amount to disproportionate attacks, and Arab governments condemned them (Al Jazeera).

perspectives.framing: Says the strike hit a legitimate military target, a Hamas command complex and its commander, and that civilian harm resulted from Hamas embedding itself under residential areas.
Calls it a massacre of civilians in a refugee camp and denies the presence of any commander, framing the attack as deliberate targeting of displaced families.
OHCHR expressed serious concern that, given the high number of civilian casualties and scale of destruction, the strikes could be disproportionate and amount to war crimes.
Amnesty International and others called for investigations into the use of heavy munitions in densely populated camps.

events.title: IDF raids Al-Shifa Hospital
events.summary: In the early hours of 15 November 2023 Israeli forces entered Al-Shifa, the largest hospital in the Gaza Strip in what the IDF called a 'targeted operation', after days of encirclement in which patients, staff and thousands of displaced people were trapped without electricity (Al Jazeera, CNN, Washington Post, NBC). The IDF said the complex concealed a Hamas command centre and displayed weapons, a laptop and an 'operational tunnel shaft', followed on 22 November by a 55-metre fortified tunnel beneath the grounds (CBS News); Hamas and hospital staff denied the claims. A WHO-led mission on 18 November described the hospital as a 'death zone' and organised evacuations (France 24); premature babies were moved to Egypt on 20 November. The raid became a central controversy over the protection of medical facilities; the Gaza Health Ministry's cumulative toll was about 11,500 by mid-November.

perspectives.framing: Says Hamas used Al-Shifa as a headquarters and hostage-holding site and that a 'precise and targeted' operation was carried out with incubators and medical supplies delivered; it argues the hospital lost its protected status.
Denies any military use of the hospital, calls the raid a war crime against patients and displaced civilians and dismisses displayed evidence as staged.

WHO said it lost contact with staff and called the situation appalling, while the UN human rights office insisted hospitals retain protection unless strict conditions are met, and called for an independent investigation.
The White House said its own intelligence indicated Hamas used Al-Shifa and tunnels beneath it to support military operations and hold hostages, while urging Israel to avoid combat inside hospitals.

events.title: Houthis seize Galaxy Leader; Red Sea shipping attacks begin
events.summary: On 19 November 2023 about ten armed Houthi fighters landed by military helicopter on the Bahamas-flagged car carrier Galaxy Leader in the southern Red Sea, seized the vessel and its 25 crew from the Philippines, Ukraine, Mexico, Romania and Bulgaria, and sailed it to the Yemeni coast near Hodeidah (PBS, UPI, French foreign ministry). The Japanese-operated, British-owned ship was linked through its registered owner to an Israeli businessman. The Houthis, who had already fired missiles and drones toward Israel in October, declared ships connected to Israel targets until the war in Gaza ended, and over the following months attacked dozens of commercial vessels with missiles, drones and small boats. Major shipping lines diverted around Africa, the United States formed the Operation Prosperity Guardian coalition in December, and US and British forces began strikes on Houthi sites in Yemen on 12 January 2024. The crew were released in January 2025.

perspectives.framing: Frames the seizures and attacks as a blockade in support of Gaza and a legitimate front of the 'axis of resistance', claiming to target only ships linked to Israel or its allies.
Called the hijacking an Iranian act of terrorism against an international vessel and part of a multi-front war orchestrated by Tehran.

Described the attacks as a threat to freedom of navigation and global commerce, organised a defensive naval coalition and later conducted strikes it described as self-defence against Houthi launch sites.
Denied directing the Houthis while praising their actions as an independent response to Israeli 'crimes' in Gaza.

events.title: Week-long truce and hostage-prisoner exchanges
events.summary: A truce brokered by Qatar, Egypt and the United States took effect on 24 November 2023, the first pause in fighting since 7 October (CNN, AJC). Initially set for four days it was extended on 27 and 30 November and lasted seven days. Hamas released 105 hostages, among them 81 Israelis and dual nationals, mostly women and children, and 24 foreign nationals, chiefly Thai workers, in daily transfers via the Red Cross through Rafah and Kerem Shalom; Israel freed 240 Palestinian prisoners, mostly women and teenagers (Time, Gulf News, AJC), and fuel and aid deliveries rose. Talks to extend the truce collapsed on 1 December amid mutual accusations of violations, Hamas fired rockets at Sderot and Israel resumed its offensive with a push into southern Gaza. The Gaza Health Ministry's cumulative toll stood at about 14,800 killed when the truce began.

perspectives.framing: Described the deal as a 'humanitarian pause' to bring hostages home, insisted the war would resume until Hamas was destroyed, and blamed Hamas for breaking the truce by failing to deliver remaining women hostages.

Presented the exchange as a victory forced by 'resistance' and the release of Palestinian 'prisoners of freedom', accused Israel of violating the truce and said it sought a permanent ceasefire and a comprehensive exchange.
Acted as chief mediator, framing the truce as a humanitarian breakthrough that could be built into a lasting ceasefire, and expressed regret when talks broke down.
Welcomed the pause, used it to scale up aid deliveries and urged that it become a full humanitarian ceasefire.

events.title: Israeli offensive in Khan Younis
events.summary: When the truce collapsed on 1 December 2023 the IDF extended its ground campaign into the southern Gaza Strip, with the 98th Division encircling and entering Khan Younis, the home city of Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar and, the IDF said, a hub of Hamas's tunnel network. Residents were told to move to al-Mawasi on the coast and to Rafah, whose population swelled to more than a million. Fighting continued through the winter, including a siege and raid on Nasser Hospital in February 2024 and the demolition of large areas. On 7 April 2024 the IDF withdrew the division, saying the Khan Younis brigade had been dismantled, thousands of militants killed and about 30 kilometres of tunnels destroyed; the Gaza Health Ministry's strip-wide toll rose from roughly 14,800 at the start of December to 33,175 by 6 April 2024.

perspectives.framing: Describes the operation as dismantling the Khan Younis Brigade and Hamas's underground command network, and as a step toward reaching Sinwar and the hostages; the April withdrawal was framed as preparation for the next phase in Rafah.
Calls the offensive an attempt to destroy a city and displace its people, and claims its fighters inflicted heavy losses on Israeli forces in urban combat.
OCHA and WHO reported the collapse of medical services, the displacement of hundreds of thousands to overcrowded Rafah and repeated strikes on shelters, and warned of famine conditions in the north.
Urged Israel to shift to lower-intensity, more targeted operations and to reduce civilian harm while continuing to support the objective of defeating Hamas.

events.title: ICJ orders provisional measures; Israel accuses UNRWA staff
events.summary: On 26 January 2024 the International Court of Justice, ruling on South Africa's application under the Genocide Convention, found it had prima facie jurisdiction and that the rights South Africa asserted were plausible. By votes of 15 to 2 and 16 to 1 it ordered Israel to take all measures to prevent acts within Article II of the Convention, to prevent and punish incitement to genocide, to enable humanitarian assistance and to report within a month; it rejected South Africa's request to suspend military operations. The same day Israel alleged that twelve UNRWA employees had taken part in the 7 October attack. UNRWA immediately dismissed nine of them and the UN opened an investigation, but the United States and more than a dozen other donors suspended funding. An independent review led by Catherine Colonna reported in April that Israel had not provided evidence for its broader claims.

perspectives.framing: Called the order a decisive victory for the rule of law, argued that Israel's conduct in Gaza is genocidal and urged states to enforce the measures.

Rejected the case as 'outrageous' and antisemitic, noted the court had not ordered a halt to the war, said it would continue to act in accordance with international law, and used the UNRWA allegations to argue the agency is compromised by Hamas.

The Secretary-General said ICJ decisions are binding, and UNRWA's Commissioner-General described the funding freeze as collective punishment of Palestinian refugees while cooperating with the OIOS investigation.
Welcomed the ruling as a recognition of the plausibility of genocide and demanded that the international community compel Israel to comply.

events.title: Deaths at aid convoy in Gaza City ('flour massacre')
events.summary: Before dawn on 29 February 2024, crowds of thousands converged on a convoy of trucks carrying flour along the coastal al-Rashid road near the Nabulsi roundabout in southwestern Gaza City, an area where the UN had warned of imminent famine. The Gaza Health Ministry said 118 people were killed and about 760 injured, mostly by Israeli gunfire. The IDF said its troops, positioned near the convoy, fired warning shots and then shot at individuals who approached them in a threatening way, killing fewer than ten, and that most of the dead were crushed in a stampede or run over by the trucks; its initial inquiry, published on 8 March, found that soldiers had not fired at the convoy itself. Survivors, video analyses and human-rights groups disputed this account, UN officials called for an independent investigation, and the deaths increased pressure for air drops and a maritime aid corridor.

perspectives.framing: Described the incident as a 'flour massacre', a deliberate attack on starving civilians, and cited it as evidence of a policy of starvation.
Says the deaths were mainly a stampede around aid trucks driven by Gazan contractors, that soldiers fired only in self-defence at people who endangered them, and that Hamas exploited the incident.

The Secretary-General condemned the incident, OHCHR said it had verified deaths from gunfire and demanded an effective investigation, and OCHA stressed the collapse of orderly aid distribution in the north.
Called the deaths 'tragic and alarming', asked Israel for answers and, days later, began air drops and announced a temporary pier for maritime aid.

events.title: UN Security Council adopts Resolution 2728 demanding a ceasefire
events.summary: On 25 March 2024 the UN Security Council adopted Resolution 2728 by 14 votes to none, with the United States abstaining, after three earlier ceasefire drafts had been vetoed by the United States or by Russia and China. The resolution demanded an immediate ceasefire for the month of Ramadan leading to a lasting and sustainable ceasefire, the immediate and unconditional release of all hostages, and the lifting of barriers to humanitarian assistance at scale. It was the Council's first ceasefire demand of the war, following resolutions 2712 and 2720 on humanitarian pauses and aid. The US abstention marked a public rift with Israel, whose prime minister cancelled a planned delegation to Washington in protest. Fighting continued and the parties disagreed over whether the resolution was binding; the Gaza Health Ministry's toll passed 32,000 that week.

perspectives.framing: The Secretary-General said the resolution must be implemented and that failure would be unforgivable; most Council members and the UN Secretariat treated it as binding on the parties.
Called the resolution a retreat from linking a ceasefire to the release of hostages, said it gave Hamas hope and vowed to continue operations until Hamas was defeated.
Welcomed the demand for a ceasefire, said it was ready for an immediate exchange of prisoners and hostages and accused Israel of defying the Council.

Explained its abstention by saying it supported the goals but objected to the absence of a condemnation of Hamas, and characterised the resolution as non-binding, a position contested by other members.

events.title: Israeli drone strikes kill seven World Central Kitchen aid workers
events.summary: On the night of 1 April 2024 three successive Israeli drone strikes hit a three-car convoy of the charity World Central Kitchen as it left a warehouse in Deir al-Balah after unloading food delivered by sea, killing seven aid workers: citizens of Australia, Poland and the United Kingdom, a US-Canadian dual national and a Palestinian driver. The vehicles were marked with the charity's logo and their movements had been coordinated with the IDF. On 5 April the IDF said the strikes were a grave mistake caused by misidentification of a suspected gunman and violations of its rules of engagement; it dismissed two officers and reprimanded three others. World Central Kitchen suspended operations in Gaza and demanded an independent inquiry. The killings prompted President Biden to press Israel on civilian protection, after which Israel announced the reopening of the Erez crossing and the port of Ashdod for aid.

perspectives.framing: Acknowledged a serious error by forces who wrongly believed a Hamas gunman was in the convoy, apologised, and pointed to disciplinary action as evidence of accountability.
Founder Jose Andres said the convoy was targeted 'systematically, car by car' despite coordination; Australia, Poland and the UK demanded full accountability and transparent investigations.
Cited the strikes as proof of deliberate targeting of aid operations and of a strategy of starvation.
President Biden said he was outraged, told Netanyahu that US support depended on concrete steps to protect civilians and aid workers, and pressed for an immediate ceasefire deal.

events.title: Israeli strike destroys Iranian consulate annex in Damascus
events.summary: On 1 April 2024 an air strike widely attributed to Israel destroyed a consular annex beside the Iranian embassy in the Mezzeh district of Damascus. Iran said seven members of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps were killed, including Brigadier General Mohammad Reza Zahedi, the senior Quds Force commander for Syria and Lebanon, and his deputy Mohammad Hadi Haji Rahimi; the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights counted 11 dead, including two Syrians and one Lebanese. Israel did not officially claim the strike, but Israeli officials said Zahedi was a legitimate military target directing attacks on Israel. Iran declared the building diplomatic premises and promised retaliation 'at the same magnitude', and on 13-14 April launched its first direct attack on Israeli territory. The strike was the most consequential of a long series of Israeli attacks on Iranian and Hezbollah targets in Syria since the Gaza war began.

perspectives.framing: Condemned the strike as an attack on sovereign diplomatic premises in violation of the Vienna Convention and a 'cowardly crime' by the 'Zionist regime', and reserved the right to respond.
Israeli officials said the building was a military facility used by the Quds Force, not a consulate, and that Zahedi was planning attacks on Israel; Israel maintained ambiguity about responsibility.
Said it had no involvement or advance notice, warned Iran against escalation and moved to reinforce regional air defences.
Denounced the strike as Israeli aggression on Syrian territory and called for international condemnation.

events.title: Iran attacks Israel directly; Israel strikes near Isfahan
events.summary: On the night of 13-14 April 2024 Iran launched what it called Operation True Promise, its first direct attack on Israeli territory, in retaliation for the Damascus consulate strike. According to the IDF, about 170 drones, more than 30 cruise missiles and more than 120 ballistic missiles were fired from Iran, with additional launches by the Houthis and Iraqi groups; Israel, the United States, Britain, France and Jordan intercepted about 99 per cent. A few ballistic missiles struck Nevatim airbase, causing light damage, and a seven-year-old Bedouin girl was seriously injured by falling shrapnel. Iran said the matter could be 'deemed concluded'. On 19 April an Israeli strike hit an air-defence radar near Isfahan, close to nuclear facilities, which Israel did not officially acknowledge and Iran played down. Both sides then stepped back from further direct exchanges until October 2024.

perspectives.framing: Framed the attack as a lawful exercise of self-defence under Article 51 of the UN Charter for the attack on its consulate, described it as calibrated and successful, and warned of a stronger response to any further Israeli action.

Called it an unprecedented act of aggression by the Iranian regime, credited a 'coalition' defence for foiling it, and said Israel would respond at a time of its choosing while showing restraint under US pressure.
Helped shoot down drones and missiles, urged Israel to 'take the win' and avoid a wider war, and coordinated new sanctions on Iran with the G7.
Said it intercepted objects violating its airspace to protect its citizens and denied acting in Israel's defence, while warning against regional escalation.

events.title: Rafah offensive; Israel seizes crossing and Philadelphi corridor
events.summary: On 6 May 2024 the IDF ordered about 100,000 people to leave eastern Rafah, where more than a million displaced Gazans had gathered, hours after Hamas announced it accepted a ceasefire proposal that Israel said differed from the one it had endorsed. On 7 May Israeli tanks seized the Palestinian side of the Rafah crossing with Egypt, which has remained closed to normal traffic since, and troops advanced into the city over the following weeks despite US warnings. On 29 May the IDF announced operational control of the entire 14-kilometre Philadelphi corridor along the Egyptian border, where it said it had found about 20 tunnels. UNRWA said on 28 May that around one million people had fled Rafah in three weeks, mostly to al-Mawasi and Khan Younis, and aid entry through the south fell sharply. Ceasefire negotiations stalled over the corridor's future.

perspectives.framing: Calls Rafah Hamas's last stronghold, the location of four remaining battalions and of smuggling tunnels into Egypt, and holds that control of the Philadelphi corridor is essential to prevent Hamas rearming.
Describes the offensive as an assault on a city of refugees, blames Israel for sabotaging the ceasefire it had accepted, and demands a full Israeli withdrawal including from the corridor.

Objected that Israel's seizure of the crossing and corridor violated the 1979 peace treaty's security annex and the 2005 crossing arrangements, refused to coordinate aid through an Israeli-held crossing and later joined the ICJ case.
Opposed a major operation in Rafah without a credible plan to protect civilians, paused a shipment of heavy bombs, then judged the operation more limited than it had feared.

events.title: ICC prosecutor seeks warrants; ICJ orders halt to Rafah offensive
events.summary: On 20 May 2024 ICC Prosecutor Karim Khan applied for arrest warrants for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Yoav Gallant on charges including starvation of civilians as a method of warfare, and for Hamas leaders Yahya Sinwar, Mohammed Deif and Ismail Haniyeh for extermination, murder, hostage-taking and sexual violence. Four days later the International Court of Justice, by 13 votes to 2, ordered Israel to immediately halt its military offensive and any other action in Rafah Governorate that could inflict on the Palestinian group in Gaza conditions of life that could bring about its physical destruction, to keep the Rafah crossing open for aid and to admit UN investigators. Israel said the order did not prohibit all operations in Rafah and continued fighting; the ICC judges issued warrants for Netanyahu, Gallant and Deif in November 2024.

perspectives.framing: Denounced the ICC application as a 'moral outrage' that equated a democracy with a 'terrorist' organisation, argued the ICC lacks jurisdiction, and read the ICJ order as permitting operations that do not create conditions of physical destruction.
Rejected the equating of 'victim and executioner' in the ICC application while welcoming the ICJ order as a demand for Israel to end its 'genocide' in Rafah.
The prosecutor said the applications followed an independent investigation and that no one is above the law; the court frames its role as impartial application of the Rome Statute.

President Biden called the ICC application outrageous and rejected any equivalence between Israel and Hamas; Washington said it did not believe Israel's Rafah operation amounted to a major ground offensive.
Called the ICJ order a clear, unambiguous instruction to stop the Rafah assault and urged enforcement through the Security Council.

events.title: Strike and fire at displaced persons' camp in Tel al-Sultan, Rafah
events.summary: On the night of 26 May 2024, two days after the ICJ order on Rafah, an Israeli air strike on the Tel al-Sultan area of northwestern Rafah set off a fire that swept through a camp of tents and shelters for displaced people near a UNRWA logistics base. The Gaza Health Ministry said 45 people were killed and more than 200 injured. The IDF said it had targeted and killed two senior Hamas officials, Yassin Rabia and Khaled Nagar, with two small precision munitions, that the site lay outside the designated humanitarian zone, and that the fire was probably caused by a secondary blast of fuel or weapons stored nearby, a claim it said was under investigation. Prime Minister Netanyahu called the deaths a 'tragic mishap'. Images of the burning camp prompted international condemnation, statements by UN human-rights experts and a UN Security Council emergency meeting.

perspectives.framing: Says the strike was precise, lawful and aimed at senior Hamas commanders, that it did not expect civilian harm and that the fire's cause was under review; it disputes descriptions of a deliberate attack on a safe zone.
Calls the attack a massacre of displaced civilians in a 'safe zone' and defiance of the ICJ, and demands international sanctions on Israel.

The Secretary-General said there was 'no safe place in Gaza' and that the horror must stop, UNRWA described the camp as sheltering civilians who had followed evacuation orders, and OHCHR called for a full investigation.
Foreign-policy chief Josep Borrell said the strike was horrifying and called for the ICJ order to be respected; France and others urged an immediate ceasefire.

events.title: Israeli raid rescues four hostages in Nuseirat
events.summary: On 8 June 2024 Israeli special forces, in a daytime operation the IDF codenamed 'Arnon', rescued four hostages, Noa Argamani, Almog Meir Jan, Andrey Kozlov and Shlomi Ziv, from two apartment buildings in the crowded Nuseirat refugee camp where they had been held since 7 October. The raid was supported by intense air and artillery strikes covering the extraction, and one police counter-terrorism officer, Arnon Zamora, was killed. The Gaza Health Ministry said 274 Palestinians were killed and 698 injured in the camp and nearby areas; the IDF said it knew of fewer than 100 casualties, including militants who fired on its forces. It was the largest single hostage rescue of the war and was celebrated in Israel, while the scale of Palestinian deaths drew condemnation from the UN and criticism from human-rights groups over the use of force in a densely populated area.

perspectives.framing: Presents the rescue as a heroic and lawful operation that proved hostages were being held in civilian homes by Hamas, and attributes civilian casualties to Hamas fighters engaging troops from within the camp.
Calls the raid the 'Nuseirat massacre', accuses Israel of killing hundreds of civilians to free four captives and says some hostages were killed by Israeli fire during the operation.
The human rights office said the deaths and injuries raised serious concern about compliance with the principles of distinction, proportionality and precaution, and called for an investigation.
Welcomed the rescue and said it had provided intelligence support, while reiterating that a ceasefire deal was the only way to free all hostages.

events.title: ICJ advisory opinion finds Israel's occupation unlawful
events.summary: On 19 July 2024 the International Court of Justice delivered an advisory opinion requested by the UN General Assembly in December 2022 on the legal consequences of Israel's policies and practices in the occupied Palestinian territory. By 11 votes to 4 the court found that Israel's continued presence in the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza is unlawful and that Israel must end it as rapidly as possible; by 14 votes to 1 it held that Israel must cease settlement activity, evacuate settlers and make reparation, and that other states must not recognise or assist the situation. It also found that Israel's policies breached the prohibition of racial segregation and apartheid under Article 3 of the CERD convention, without adjudicating which term applied. Although non-binding, it was the court's most sweeping statement on the occupation; the General Assembly in September 2024 demanded that Israel end its presence within twelve months.

perspectives.framing: Rejected the opinion as one-sided, 'a decision of lies' that ignored Israel's security needs and the 7 October attack, and asserted that the Jewish people are not occupiers in their own land, using the term Judea and Samaria for the West Bank.
Hailed a historic ruling confirming that the occupation and settlements are illegal and demanded that states impose sanctions and end arms sales to Israel.

The Secretary-General transmitted the opinion to the General Assembly, which endorsed it; UN officials described the finding as consistent with long-standing UN positions on the illegality of settlements.

Said it was concerned by the breadth of the opinion, argued it would complicate efforts toward a negotiated two-state solution and rejected the idea that the court could compel a unilateral withdrawal.

events.title: Majdal Shams strike; Fuad Shukr and Ismail Haniyeh killed
events.summary: On 27 July 2024 a rocket struck a football pitch in the Druze town of Majdal Shams in the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights, killing 12 children and teenagers, the deadliest attack on Israeli-held territory since 7 October. Israel and the United States said it was a Hezbollah Falaq-1 rocket; Hezbollah denied responsibility. On 30 July an Israeli strike on an apartment building in Haret Hreik in Beirut's southern suburbs killed Fuad Shukr, Hezbollah's most senior military commander, and, according to Lebanese officials, several civilians including children. Hours later, in the early hours of 31 July, Hamas political chief Ismail Haniyeh was killed by an explosion at a guesthouse in Tehran after attending President Pezeshkian's inauguration; Iran and Hamas blamed Israel, which did not comment at the time. Iran and Hezbollah vowed revenge, and Hezbollah launched a large barrage on 25 August after Israeli pre-emptive strikes.

perspectives.framing: Held Hezbollah responsible for a massacre of children and described the killing of Shukr as the response; it maintained ambiguity on Haniyeh while officials said all Hamas leaders were legitimate targets.
Denied firing at Majdal Shams, suggesting an Israeli interceptor was responsible, mourned Shukr as a 'great commander' and promised a definite response to the Beirut strike.
Called Haniyeh's killing a violation of its sovereignty and a 'cowardly' assassination by the 'Zionist regime', and Supreme Leader Khamenei said Israel would face harsh punishment.
Mourned Haniyeh as a 'martyr' and said the assassination would not go unanswered, while continuing ceasefire talks under Yahya Sinwar, who was named as his successor.
Backed Israel's attribution of the Majdal Shams strike to Hezbollah, urged restraint on all sides and said it had no advance knowledge of the Tehran operation.

events.title: Gaza Health Ministry death toll passes 40,000
events.summary: On 15 August 2024 the Gaza Health Ministry reported that 40,005 Palestinians had been killed and 92,401 injured since 7 October 2023, a figure that UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk cited while stressing that thousands more were believed buried under rubble. The ministry's tally does not distinguish combatants from civilians; it said most of the identified dead were women and children. Israel disputes the composition of the toll: the IDF said by that month that it had killed some 17,000 Hamas and other militants, and Israeli officials questioned the ministry's methods, although Israeli intelligence assessments cited by the press regarded the overall figure as broadly reliable. Independent studies published in The Lancet argued the true number of direct and indirect deaths was likely higher. The IDF reported more than 300 of its soldiers killed in Gaza since the ground invasion began.

perspectives.framing: Presents the toll as a count of 'martyrs' compiled from hospital records and verified family reports, most of them civilians, and says the real total is higher because of the missing.

Argues that Hamas controls the ministry and inflates or misclassifies deaths, that a large share of the dead are combatants, and that the civilian-to-combatant ratio is lower than in comparable urban wars.

OHCHR High Commissioner Volker Turk called the 40,000 figure a grim milestone and urged an end to the fighting; UN agencies use the ministry's numbers, which they have found credible in past conflicts, while noting they cannot independently verify them.

Studies in The Lancet found the ministry's data internally consistent and suggested that direct deaths were under-recorded and that indirect deaths from disease and hunger would raise the total substantially.

events.title: Humanitarian pauses agreed for Gaza polio vaccination campaign
events.summary: On 29 August 2024 the World Health Organization announced that Israel had agreed to a series of localised humanitarian pauses to allow a mass polio vaccination campaign in Gaza, after the first confirmed case of poliovirus in the territory in 25 years, a ten-month-old child in Deir al-Balah, was reported in August and the virus had been detected in wastewater in July. The plan, negotiated by WHO and UNICEF with COGAT, the Israeli military coordination body, and accepted by Hamas, provided three-day pauses in fighting from 6 am to 3 pm in central, southern and then northern Gaza in turn, beginning on 1 September. The campaign aimed to reach more than 640,000 children under ten with two doses of novel oral polio vaccine; the first round, run from 1 to 12 September, reached about 560,000 children. It was the first agreed pause in fighting since the November 2023 truce.

perspectives.framing: WHO and UNICEF described the pauses as a narrow humanitarian necessity, not a ceasefire, and warned that polio's return reflected the collapse of water and sanitation in Gaza.
COGAT said it coordinated the campaign and the entry of vaccines as part of its humanitarian efforts, while insisting that operations against Hamas would continue outside the agreed windows.
Said it would cooperate with the campaign and called for a full ceasefire, blaming Israel's destruction of infrastructure for the outbreak.
Welcomed the arrangement and pressed both parties to observe the pauses and to reach a broader ceasefire deal.

boundaryChanges.description: Israeli ground forces enter the northern Gaza Strip (Beit Hanoun, Beit Lahia, Jabalia and the coast); by mid-November the IDF holds most of the area north and west of Gaza City and has reached the coast south of the city, cutting the Strip in two along what becomes the Netzarim corridor. Hamas's civil administration ceases to function in the north.

IDF announces it has encircled Gaza City and split the Strip between north and south; the east-west Netzarim corridor south of Gaza City is progressively fortified into a permanent Israeli-controlled zone with checkpoints controlling movement between the two halves.

After the truce collapses the IDF extends ground operations to Khan Younis and the central camps; a widening belt roughly one kilometre deep inside Gaza's perimeter fence is cleared of buildings to form an Israeli-controlled buffer zone along the whole eastern and northern edge of the Strip.

The IDF's 98th Division withdraws from Khan Younis, leaving the south to Hamas administration again while Israeli forces retain the Netzarim corridor, the perimeter buffer zone and control of the north.
Israeli forces seize the Gaza side of the Rafah crossing with Egypt; the crossing closes to normal traffic and remains under Israeli military control for the rest of the era.

The IDF announces operational control of the entire Philadelphi corridor along the Gaza-Egypt border, adding a second Israeli-controlled strip inside Gaza; the question of withdrawal from this corridor becomes a central obstacle in ceasefire talks.

No change of territorial control on the Israel-Lebanon front during this era, but both sides empty their border zones: Israel evacuates communities up to about 5 km from the Blue Line and Hezbollah's presence south of the Litani persists until the September-October 2024 escalation.

The ten events from 2023-10-07 to the 24-30 November 2023 truce were each corroborated on date, place and key facts by >= 2 publishers in search-result content and are set verified:true, with their sources replaced by URLs that appeared in those results (all 'accessedDate' 2026-09-14 entries). Each was corroborated on date, place and headline facts/figures by >= 2 publishers in search-result content and is set verified:true; all sources were replaced with URLs that appeared in those results (accessedDate 2026-09-14). 7 October 2023 toll: Israel initially cited about 1,400 dead, revised to about 1,200 in November 2023 after some unidentified remains were determined to be attackers; the civilian/soldier split (roughly 800 civilians and 350-400 security personnel) varies by compiler. The hostage count was reported as about 240 in late 2023 and standardised as 251 in 2024; both figures appear in official Israeli material.

Al-Ahli Hospital (17 Oct 2023): the cause and the toll remain contested. The Gaza Health Ministry's 471 dead has never been independently verified; US intelligence estimated 100-300; HRW and several media forensic analyses judged the blast consistent with a Palestinian rocket, which Hamas and Islamic Jihad reject. The entry presents all attributions without adjudicating.

Jabalia (31 Oct-1 Nov 2023): casualty figures range from 'more than 50' (Indonesian Hospital director) to several hundred killed and injured (Hamas-run interior ministry); the IDF's claim that Ibrahim Biari and 'dozens' of fighters were killed is unverified.

Truce exchanges (24-30 Nov 2023): the 105 hostages released are variously counted as 81 Israelis and dual nationals plus 24 foreign nationals, or 110 including four released before and after the pause; 240 Palestinian prisoners is the most common figure.

Flour massacre (29 Feb 2024): the Gaza Health Ministry's 118 dead (initially 112) and the IDF's finding that most died in a crush are irreconcilable on current evidence; OHCHR said it verified gunshot deaths but no independent total exists.

Nuseirat (8 June 2024): 274 killed (Gaza Health Ministry) versus 'fewer than 100' (IDF); the ministry's daily report of 9 June recorded 283 deaths in 24 hours strip-wide, consistent with but not proof of its figure.
Tel al-Sultan (26 May 2024): the fire's cause (IDF munitions versus a secondary explosion of stored weapons) is unresolved; the 45-dead figure is the ministry's.

Haniyeh (31 July 2024): Israel did not acknowledge the killing until December 2024, so contemporaneous attribution rests on Iranian and Hamas statements and later reporting; the method (a pre-planted device versus a projectile) was reported differently by Iran's IRGC and by Western press.
Majdal Shams (27 July 2024): Hezbollah denies firing the rocket; Israel and the US attribute it to Hezbollah. The entry records both positions.

Cumulative Gaza toll: Gaza Health Ministry figures do not distinguish combatants; the IDF's estimate of about 17,000 militants killed by mid-2024 is not independently verifiable and Israeli officials have given differing numbers. The Lancet correspondence of July 2024 projecting up to 186,000 direct and indirect deaths is an extrapolation, not a count, and is cited only as a claim by academic authors.

Displacement: the 1.9 million figure is an OCHA/UNRWA estimate that remained roughly constant from December 2023 to mid-2024 while the population of individual areas changed dramatically; it does not capture repeated displacement. Israeli evacuation numbers (northern border about 60,000; total including Gaza envelope variously 120,000-250,000) also vary by source.

Damascus consulate strike (1 April 2024): Iran gives 7 IRGC dead; the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights reported up to 16 including Syrian and Hezbollah personnel; Israel never officially claimed the strike.

Iran attack (13-14 April 2024): projectile counts come from the IDF; Iran gave lower figures for missiles launched and claimed greater damage at Nevatim than Israel acknowledged. The 19 April Isfahan strike was never officially claimed by Israel.
